findings.description: The EC2 instance's user_data embeds a plaintext AWS access key ID and secret access key, which are stored in instance metadata and readable by anyone with access to the instance or the user-data endpoint. These long-lived credentials should be removed and replaced with an IAM instance profile.

The security group exposes SSH (port 22) to 0.0.0.0/0, allowing brute-force and credential-stuffing attacks from the entire internet. SSH should be restricted to a trusted CIDR or reached via a bastion/SSM.

HTTP (port 80) is open to 0.0.0.0/0. While common for public web servers, combined with the plaintext credentials in user data this broad exposure increases the attack surface; it is acceptable only if the service is intended to be public.
The egress rule permits all protocols and all ports to 0.0.0.0/0, which allows a compromised instance to exfiltrate data or reach any external host. Egress should be scoped to required destinations.
map_public_ip_on_launch is true, so every instance launched into this subnet receives a publicly routable IP and is directly reachable from the internet, removing a layer of network isolation.
map_public_ip_on_launch is true, so instances in this subnet automatically get public IPs and are exposed directly to the internet.
The S3 bucket used for VPC flow logs has no server-side encryption configuration, so flow-log data (including source/destination IPs and traffic metadata) is stored unencrypted at rest.
The bucket has no aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block and no explicit ACL restriction, leaving it potentially subject to public exposure. A public access block and ownership controls should be applied.
The EBS volume has no encryption specified, so data on the attached disk is stored unencrypted and can be read if the volume or a snapshot is exfiltrated.
The EBS snapshot is created without encryption, so a full copy of the disk contents is stored unencrypted and could be shared or restored by an attacker with snapshot access.

The instance does not set metadata_options to require IMDSv2 (http_tokens = "required"), leaving it vulnerable to SSRF-based credential theft via the IMDSv1 endpoint, which is especially dangerous given the credentials in user data.
